title: Isogeny-based Cryptography Wiki
text: Welcome to the Isogeny-based Cryptography Wiki. This site serves as an open-source, mathematically rigorous, and accessible repository of knowledge detailing post-quantum cryptographic protocols built on the hardness of finding isogenies between elliptic curves.

title: FESTA
text: FESTA is a public-key encryption (PKE) protocol that creatively repurposes the devastating attacks on the SIDH protocol. While SIDH’s security was compromised by torsion-point attacks when auxiliary torsion information is revealed, FESTA relies on a novel trapdoor function where these very attacks are leveraged by the legitimate trapdoor holder to invert a one-way function [BaMaPo23].

title: FESTA
text: FESTA is a public-key encryption (PKE) protocol that creatively repurposes the devastating attacks on the SIDH protocol. title: FESTA
text:
2 Protocol Design
The foundation of FESTA is an injective trapdoor function evaluated over supersingular elliptic curves. By scaling the revealed torsion points with a secret matrix, FESTA prevents malicious attackers from utilizing the SIDH attacks. Using standard transformations (like OAEP), this trapdoor mechanism enables the construction of an efficient IND-CCA secure PKE in the Quantum Random Oracle Model (QROM).

2.1 Global Parameters

\(p\): A prime defined as \(2^b d_1 (d_A)_{sf} d_2 f - 1\), where \(d_1, d_2, d_A\) are smooth numbers and \((d_A)_{sf}\) is the square free part of \(d_A\).
\(E_0\): A starting supersingular elliptic curve defined over \(\mathbb{F}_{p^2}\) (chosen with \(j(E_0) \neq 0, 1728\) to avoid non-trivial automorphisms).
\(\langle P_b, Q_b \rangle = E_0[2^b]\): A canonical basis for the \(2^b\)-torsion on \(E_0\).
\(\mathcal{M}_b\): A set of commutative, invertible diagonal matrices over \((\mathbb{Z}/2^b\mathbb{Z})^\times\) modulo \(\langle -I_2 \rangle\).



2.2 Setup and Key Generation
The trapdoor key generation works as follows:

Compute a secret \(d_A\)-isogeny \(\varphi_A: E_0 \rightarrow E_A\).
Sample a random matrix \(\mathbf{A} \in \mathcal{M}_b\).
Calculate the scaled torsion images on \(E_A\): \[ \begin{pmatrix} R_A \\ S_A \end{pmatrix} = \mathbf{A} \begin{pmatrix} \varphi_A(P_b) \\ \varphi_A(Q_b) \end{pmatrix} \]


Secret Key (Trapdoor): \((\mathbf{A}, \varphi_A)\).
Public Key: \((E_A, R_A, S_A)\).



2.3 Function Evaluation (Forward Direction)
To evaluate the one-way function on an input consisting of two isogenies \(\varphi_1: E_0 \rightarrow E_1\) (degree \(d_1\)), \(\varphi_2: E_A \rightarrow E_2\) (degree \(d_2\)), and a matrix \(\mathbf{B} \in \mathcal{M}_b\):

Compute \(\varphi_1: E_0 \rightarrow E_1\) and \(\varphi_2: E_A \rightarrow E_2\).
Scale the torsion basis images under \(\varphi_1\) by \(\mathbf{B}\): \[ \begin{pmatrix} R_1 \\ S_1 \end{pmatrix} = \mathbf{B} \begin{pmatrix} \varphi_1(P_b) \\ \varphi_1(Q_b) \end{pmatrix} \]
Scale the public torsion parameters under \(\varphi_2\) by \(\mathbf{B}\): \[ \begin{pmatrix} R_2 \\ S_2 \end{pmatrix} = \mathbf{B} \begin{pmatrix} \varphi_2(R_A) \\ \varphi_2(S_A) \end{pmatrix} \]


Output: The tuple \((E_1, R_1, S_1, E_2, R_2, S_2)\).

Without the knowledge of \(\mathbf{A}\), the scaling by \(\mathbf{B}\) (and natively \(\mathbf{A}\)) thoroughly obfuscates the torsion point information, blocking the SIDH attack machinery.


2.4 Trapdoor Inversion
The trapdoor owner can invert the function by utilizing the commutativity of matrices \(\mathbf{A}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\):

Undo the secret scaling on \(E_2\) by applying \(d_1 \mathbf{A}^{-1}\): \[ \begin{pmatrix} R_2' \\ S_2' \end{pmatrix} = d_1 \mathbf{A}^{-1} \begin{pmatrix} R_2 \\ S_2 \end{pmatrix} \] Because \(\mathbf{A}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\) commute, this effectively isolates the scaling to just \(\mathbf{B}\), bridging the torsion mappings between \(E_1\) and \(E_2\).
The resulting points reflect the exact unscaled images of \(R_1, S_1\) under the bridging isogeny \(\psi := \varphi_2 \circ \varphi_A \circ \hat{\varphi}_1\).
Invoke an arbitrary torsion-point attack (e.g., Kani’s criterion generalizing to higher dimensions via (2,2)-isogenies) on \((E_1, R_1, S_1, E_2, R_2', S_2')\) to efficiently compute \(\psi\).
Reconstruct the original kernels of \(\varphi_1, \varphi_2\) and the matrix \(\mathbf{B}\) from \(\psi\).

title: FESTA
text:
3 Security Assumptions
FESTA introduces generalized hardness assumptions for the scaled-torsion setting:

Decisional Isogeny with Scaled-Torsion (DIST): Distinguishing a curve and its scaled torsion images (via matrix \(A\)) from a random supersingular curve and random basis points.
Computational Isogeny with Scaled-Torsion (CIST): Extracting the isogeny \(\varphi\) given \(E_0, E_1\), the domain basis, and the scaled target basis \(\mathbf{A}(\varphi(P_0), \varphi(Q_0))^T\).
Computational Isogeny with Double Scaled-Torsion (CIST\(^2\)): Recovering two distinct isogenies \(\varphi, \varphi'\) given two instances of scaled target bases that use the same scaling matrix \(\mathbf{A}\).

title: QFESTA
text:
QFESTA (Quaternion Fast Encapsulation from Supersingular Torsion Attacks) is a new isogeny-based public-key encryption (PKE) and key encapsulation mechanism (KEM) based on the FESTA protocol [NaOn24].
FESTA uses the SIDH attack machinery for decryption, which natively imposes strong smoothness constraints on the degrees of the underlying isogenies (\(d_A, d_1, d_2\)), forcing them to be large and leading to significant data sizes and computational overhead. To circumvent these limitations, QFESTA introduces a novel technique leveraging quaternion algebras to compute the codomain and point images of non-smooth degree isogenies from a special starting curve. This eliminates the smoothness restriction for degrees \(d_A\) and \(d_1\), vastly shrinking parameter sizes.

title: QFESTA
text:
2 Protocol Design
The main innovation in QFESTA’s design is the sub-algorithm RandIsogImages, which evaluates non-smooth degree isogenies using Kani’s lemma and quaternion endomorphisms. Finally, to achieve indistinguishability against chosen ciphertext attacks (IND-CCA) in the quantum random oracle model (QROM), the core One-Way Chosen Plaintext Attack (OW-CPA) secure PKE is wrapped using the Fujisaki-Okamoto (\(FO^{\not\perp}\)) transform.

2.1 The RandIsogImages Algorithm
Given a special supersingular elliptic curve \(E_0/\mathbb{F}_{p^2}\) with \(j\)-invariant 1728, its known maximal order \(\mathcal{O}_0 \cong \text{End}(E_0)\), and an target non-smooth isogeny degree \(d\):
E0EA¿:d¡isogeny½:(D¡d)¡isogeny®

A smooth integer \(D = 2^{3a}\) is chosen such that \(E_0[D] \subset E_0(\mathbb{F}_{p^2})\) and \(D - d \approx p\).
The algorithm computes an element \(\alpha \in \mathcal{O}_0\) with a reduced norm of \(d(D-d)\) using an extension of Cornacchia’s algorithm (FullRepresentInteger).
The quaternion element \(\alpha\) is formally decomposed into \(\hat{\rho} \circ \tau\), where \(\tau\) and \(\rho\) are isogenies of degrees \(d\) and \(D-d\), respectively.
By leveraging Kani’s lemma (via SIDH attack components like CodomainByKani and EvalByKani), the algorithm extracts the codomain of \(\tau\) and the images of arbitrary torsion points under \(\tau\) entirely through (2,2)-isogeny chains.



2.2 Key Generation

Parameters: Uses a system parameter set containing \((p, a, b, d_{A,1}, d_1, E_0, \mathcal{O}_0, P_0, Q_0)\).
Secret Isogeny \(\phi_A\): A random non-smooth degree \(d_{A,1}\)-isogeny is generated from \(E_0 \to E_{A,1}\) via RandIsogImages, followed by a random \(3^b\)-isogeny to the final public curve \(E_A\).
Masking: Torsion points on \(E_A\) are masked using a randomly sampled matrix \(\mathbf{A} \in M_2(\mathbb{Z}/2^{3a}\mathbb{Z})\).
Keys: The public key pk consists of the curve \(E_A\) and the masked points \((R_A, S_A)\). The secret key sk contains the isogeny path representations and the matrix \(\mathbf{A}\).



2.3 Encryption and Decryption

Encryption: To encrypt a message \(m \in \{0, 1\}^{3a-2}\), the sender encodes it into a diagonal masking matrix \(\mathbf{B} = \text{diag}(s_B, s_B^{-1})\) where \(s_B = 2m+1\). The sender generates a \(d_1\)-isogeny to a curve \(E_1\) using RandIsogImages and a \(3^{2b}\)-isogeny from \(E_A\) to \(E_2\). The output ciphertext encapsulates these curves and points masked by \(\mathbf{B}\).
Decryption: Utilizing the secret isogeny \(\phi_A\) and the EvalByKani algorithm, the receiver can reconstruct the commutative diagrams necessary to unmask the points and solve a discrete logarithm (via Weil or Tate pairings) to retrieve the matrix \(\mathbf{B}\), and consequently the message \(m\).

title: QFESTA
text:
3 Security Assumptions
The core OW-CPA security of the QFESTA PKE relies on specialized variants of FESTA’s distinguishing and computational problems.

Pseudorandomness of RandIsogImages: The foundational assumption assumes that the codomain elliptic curve \(E_1\) and its mapped torsion points \((P_1, Q_1)\) produced by RandIsogImages are computationally indistinguishable from a tuple drawn uniformly at random from valid configurations.
Variant DIST Problem: The security proof extends this to the public keys themselves, assuming an adversary cannot distinguish the legitimate masked points \((R_A, S_A)\) on \(E_A\) from uniformly random torsion points.
Hardness of Isogeny Recovery: Finding the secret isogenies (\(\phi_A, \phi_1, \phi_2\)) given the degrees (\(d_A, d_1, d_2\)) requires \(O(2^{\lambda})\) operations classically and \(O(2^{\lambda/2})\) operations via quantum attacks (using Grover’s algorithm or meet-in-the-middle strategies), satisfying the targeted security levels.
Resistance to Castryck-Vercauteren Attack: This specific polynomial-time attack is circumvented by carefully selecting the public basis \((P_0, Q_0) \in E_0[2^{3a}]\). The protocol computes endomorphism representations of these points and verifies that the shortest vector in the resulting Euclidean lattice has a norm greater than \(2^{1.5\lambda}\), guaranteeing security against \(\lambda\)-bit complexity attacks.

title: CSI-FiSh
text:
CSI-FiSh (Commutative Supersingular Isogeny Signatures with Fiat-Shamir) is an efficient isogeny-based digital signature scheme introduced by Beullens, Kleinjung, and Vercauteren [BeKlVe19].
The primary hurdle in building efficient signatures from the CSIDH group action is that evaluating the group action can be slow, and the structure of the class group \(\text{Cl}(R)\) is generally unknown. CSI-FiSh circumvents this by working with a specific parameter set where the class group can be fully computed.
CSI-FiSh relies on the same hardness assumptions outlined in the CSIDH.

title: CSI-FiSh

CSI-FiSh (Commutative Supersingular Isogeny Signatures with Fiat-Shamir) is an efficient isogeny-based digital signature scheme introduced by Beullens, Kleinjung, and Vercauteren [BeKlVe19].
The primary hurdle in building efficient signatures from the CSIDH group action is that evaluating the group action can be slow, and the structure of the class group \(\text{Cl}(R)\) is generally unknown. CSI-FiSh circumvents this by working with a specific parameter set where the class group can be fully computed.
CSI-FiSh relies on the same hardness assumptions outlined in the CSIDH.

title: CSI-FiSh
text:
2 Key Mechanism
By computing the exact structure of \(\text{Cl}(R)\) for a 512-bit prime \(p\), CSI-FiSh can perform fast, uniform sampling of elements. This allows a direct, efficient adaptation of the classical Fiat-Shamir transform to the isogeny setting.

Underlying Hard Problem: The security relies on the hardness of finding paths between supersingular elliptic curves (the Vectorization Problem), similar to the security assumptions laid out in the foundational CSIDH protocol.

title: SIDH
text:
It was a NIST PQC competition candidate but is now broken.

The Supersingular Isogeny Diffie-Hellman (SIDH) scheme is a public-key exchange protocol designed to be secure against quantum computer attacks. Diffie-Hellman-type protocols inherently require commutativity to establish a shared secret [JaFe11]. SIDH overcomes the noncommutativity of the supersingular endomorphism ring by having parties transmit the images of specific torsion bases under their secret isogenies as auxiliary input.

title: SIDH
text:
2 Protocol Design
The protocol dictates that Alice and Bob conduct random walks on two distinct isogeny graphs (of degrees \(\ell_A\) and \(\ell_B\) respectively) and use auxiliary points to arrive at an isomorphic destination curve.
E0EAEBEBAEABkker(ÁA)=h[mA]PA+[nA]QAiÁA(PB);ÁA(QB)ÁB(PA);ÁB(QA)ker(ÁB)=h[mB]PB+[nB]QBiker(Á0B)=h[mB]ÁA(PB)+[nB]ÁA(QB)iker(Á0A)=h[mA]ÁB(PA)+[nA]ÁB(QA)i

2.1 Public Parameters Setup

The scheme is defined over a finite field \(\mathbb{F}_{p^2}\) where the prime \(p\) is of the form \(p = \ell_A^{e_A} \ell_B^{e_B} \cdot f \pm 1\). Here, \(\ell_A\) and \(\ell_B\) are small primes (typically 2 and 3), and \(f\) is a small cofactor.
A base supersingular curve \(E_0\) defined over \(\mathbb{F}_{p^2}\) is fixed as a public parameter.
Two sets of bases are published: \(\{P_A, Q_A\}\), which generates the torsion group \(E_0[\ell_A^{e_A}]\), and \(\{P_B, Q_B\}\), which generates \(E_0[\ell_B^{e_B}]\).



2.2 Alice’s Key Generation

Alice chooses two random elements \(m_A, n_A \in \mathbb{Z}/\ell_A^{e_A}\mathbb{Z}\), ensuring they are not both divisible by \(\ell_A\).
She computes a secret isogeny \(\phi_A : E_0 \rightarrow E_A\) characterized by the kernel \(K_A := \langle [m_A]P_A + [n_A]Q_A \rangle\).
To allow Bob to complete the exchange, she evaluates her secret isogeny on Bob’s basis points, yielding \(\phi_A(P_B)\) and \(\phi_A(Q_B)\).
Alice’s public key sent to Bob is the tuple \((E_A, \phi_A(P_B), \phi_A(Q_B))\).



2.3 Bob’s Key Generation

Bob correspondingly selects random elements \(m_B, n_B \in \mathbb{Z}/\ell_B^{e_B}\mathbb{Z}\).
He computes his secret isogeny \(\phi_B : E_0 \rightarrow E_B\) defined by the kernel \(K_B := \langle [m_B]P_B + [n_B]Q_B \rangle\).
Bob evaluates his isogeny on Alice’s basis points to produce \(\phi_B(P_A)\) and \(\phi_B(Q_A)\).
Bob’s public key sent to Alice is the tuple \((E_B, \phi_B(P_A), \phi_B(Q_A))\).



2.4 Shared Key Derivation

Upon receiving Bob’s public key, Alice calculates a new isogeny \(\phi'_A : E_B \rightarrow E_{AB}\) utilizing the evaluated points Bob sent. Her new kernel is \(\langle [m_A]\phi_B(P_A) + [n_A]\phi_B(Q_A) \rangle\).
Concurrently, Bob computes a new isogeny \(\phi'_B : E_A \rightarrow E_{BA}\) utilizing Alice’s evaluated points, with the kernel \(\langle [m_B]\phi_A(P_B) + [n_B]\phi_A(Q_B) \rangle\).
The curves \(E_{AB}\) and \(E_{BA}\) are isomorphic, allowing both parties to establish a common shared key by computing the \(j\)-invariant \(j(E_{AB})\).

title: SIDH
text:
3 Security Assumptions

Hardness Problem: The scheme relies on the conjectured difficulty of finding an isogeny between two supersingular elliptic curves.
Auxiliary Input Security: A unique characteristic of SIDH is the publication of the evaluated torsion basis points (the auxiliary input required for commutativity). The authors state that providing these outputs does not appear to make the underlying problem of finding the secret isogenies any easier.
Resistance to Quantum Group Actions: Because the protocol is not fundamentally based on an abelian group action, it is completely immune to the subexponential quantum attacks that rendered ordinary isogeny networks insecure.

title: CSIDH
text: CSIDH is a post-quantum commutative group action that enables efficient non-interactive key exchange [CLMP18]. The construction adapts the layout of earlier cryptosystems proposed by Couveignes and Rostovtsev-Stolbunov, but replaces the use of ordinary elliptic curves with supersingular elliptic curves defined over a large prime field \(\mathbb{F}_p\) . A key advantage of using supersingular curves over \(\mathbb{F}_p\) (for \(p \ge 5\)) is that they always have exactly \(p + 1\) rational points, which trivially yields the highly composite order needed for efficiency.

title: CSIDH
text:
2 Protocol Design
The core of the CSIDH protocol is based on the free and transitive action of the ideal-class group \(cl(\mathcal{O})\) on the set of \(\mathbb{F}_p\)-isomorphism classes of supersingular elliptic curves with an \(\mathbb{F}_p\)-rational endomorphism ring isomorphic to \(\mathcal{O}\).

2.1 Parameters
The protocol fixes a large prime \(p\) of the form \(4 \cdot \ell_1 \cdots \ell_n - 1\), where \(\ell_i\) are small, distinct odd primes. The base curve is defined as \(E_0 : y^2 = x^3 + x\) over \(\mathbb{F}_p\). The requirement that \(p \equiv 3 \pmod 4\) ensures that \(E_0\) is supersingular and permits the use of efficient Montgomery arithmetic.


2.2 Endomorphism Ring & Isogenies
The Frobenius endomorphism \(\pi\) of \(E_0\) satisfies \(\pi^2 = -p\), giving an \(\mathbb{F}_p\)-rational endomorphism ring of \(\mathcal{O} = \mathbb{Z}[\pi]\). Because \(\pi^2 - 1 \equiv 0 \pmod{\ell_i}\), the ideals \(\ell_i\mathcal{O}\) split into Elkies primes \(\mathfrak{l}_i = (\ell_i, \pi - 1)\) and \(\bar{\mathfrak{l}}_i = (\ell_i, \pi + 1)\). The isogenies for \(\mathfrak{l}_i\) can be evaluated efficiently because their kernels are generated by points of order \(\ell_i\) that lie in the kernel of \(\pi - 1\), meaning they are rational over the base field \(\mathbb{F}_p\).


2.3 Private Key
A private key is constructed as an exponent vector \((e_1, \dots, e_n)\) with each \(e_i \in \{-m, \dots, m\}\), representing the ideal class \([\mathfrak{l}_1^{e_1} \mathfrak{l}_2^{e_2} \cdots \mathfrak{l}_n^{e_n}] \in cl(\mathcal{O})\).


2.4 Public Key
An individual’s public key (e.g., Alice’s key \(A\)) is the Montgomery coefficient of the curve \(E_A : y^2 = x^3 + Ax^2 + x\), which is obtained by applying the action of the secret key \([a]\) to the base curve \(E_0\).


2.5 Key Exchange
When Alice receives Bob’s public key \(B\), she first verifies that the curve \(E_B\) is supersingular. She then applies her secret ideal class action \([\mathfrak{a}]\) to compute \([\mathfrak{a}]E_B = [\mathfrak{a}][\mathfrak{b}]E_0\). The shared secret is the unique Montgomery coefficient \(S\) corresponding to the combined curve \([\mathfrak{a}][\mathfrak{b}]E_0\).

title: CSIDH
text:
3 Security Assumptions
The security of the CSIDH protocol relies on the hardness of an isogeny-finding problem analogous to the classical discrete logarithm problem.

3.1 Key Recovery Problem
The fundamental computational assumption is that given two supersingular elliptic curves \(E\) and \(E'\) over \(\mathbb{F}_p\) with the same \(\mathbb{F}_p\)-rational endomorphism ring \(\mathcal{O}\), it is computationally infeasible to find an ideal \(\mathfrak{a}\) such that \([\mathfrak{a}]E = E'\).


3.2 Quantum Security
Breaking the scheme translates to solving an instance of the abelian hidden-shift problem. This problem can be addressed using subexponential-time quantum algorithms, such as those proposed by Kuperberg. The precise asymptotic complexity depends heavily on the cost of computing the isogeny oracle; combinations of algorithms yield bounds in the realm of \(L_p[1/2, 1/\sqrt{2}]\).


3.3 Chosen-Ciphertext Security
Because CSIDH naturally affords efficient public-key validation, it avoids vulnerabilities related to the reuse of dishonest keys. This validation allows CSIDH to securely achieve non-interactive key exchange without resorting to additional chosen-ciphertext attack (CCA) transformations like the Fujisaki-Okamoto transform.
